standard.title: Federation and democracy
standard.description: significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation, the Constitution and democratic system of government
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students explain the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including elections and the roles of elected representatives. Students understand democratic values and electoral features.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation, the Constitution and democratic system of government, identifying the origins and influences that shaped Australia's constitutional framework.

nodes.label: The path to Federation — key individuals and events
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the roles of key individuals and events in Australia's path to Federation, including Henry Parkes, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin, the Tenterfield Oration and the Corowa Conference.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the role of one key individual and one key event in Australia's path to Federation.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the roles of key individuals (Henry Parkes, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin, George Reid, John Quick) and key events (Tenterfield Oration, Corowa Conference, 1898–1900 referendums) in Australia's path to Federation.
wider: Investigate the perspectives of those who opposed Federation and explain their objections — examining why Federation was not universally welcomed
Explore the role of women and First Nations Australians in the Federation debate, and assess whose voices were included or excluded from the constitutional drafting process
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding the actors and events that drove Federation, students cannot explain why the Constitution was designed as it was, or what ideas the founders drew on. This factual and narrative foundation is the prerequisite for the constitutional and democratic analysis in subsequent nodes.

response_modes.reason: Use a timeline of key events alongside brief profiles of key individuals to build the chronological foundation before moving to analysis of the ideas and influences that shaped Federation.

success_criteria: Students identify at least two key individuals and two key events in Australia's path to Federation.
Students explain the role each individual or event played in the Federation process.

nodes.label: The ideas and influences behind Australia's Constitution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key ideas and influences behind Australia's Constitution, including the influence of the Westminster system, the US federal model and the Magna Carta.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one idea or influence that shaped the design of Australia's Constitution.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of ideas and influences that shaped Australia's Constitution: origins in Magna Carta, the English Civil War and Westminster system (explaining constitutional monarchy and separation of powers); the influence of the American federal model (Washington system) on Andrew Clark's first draft.
wider: Compare the Australian Constitution with the Westminster system and the US Constitution, identifying specific features borrowed from each
Investigate what separation of powers means in practice — examine a real example of the legislature, executive and judiciary operating independently to illustrate the concept

response_modes.reason: The international influences on the Australian Constitution (British and American) are best understood comparatively — students need enough context about each source to understand what was borrowed and why.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing Australian constitutional design with its British and American origins is a rich comparative direction that connects to ongoing constitutional questions and provides substantive historical context for understanding Australian democracy.
success_criteria: Students identify at least two influences on the design of Australia's Constitution.
Students explain how each influence shaped a specific feature of the Constitution (e.g. separation of powers, constitutional monarchy).

nodes.label: Australia's democratic system of government
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key features of Australia's democratic system of government that emerged from Federation, including the constitutional monarchy, federal structure and separation of powers.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two key features of Australia's system of government established at Federation.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the key features of Australia's democratic system of government: constitutional monarchy, federal structure (Commonwealth and States), separation of powers (legislative, executive, judiciary), and how these features are embedded in the Constitution.
wider: Investigate the Australian Constitution document itself — identify specific sections that establish key features of government and explain what each means in practice
Explore the ongoing debate about Australia becoming a republic, and assess what would need to change in the Constitution and system of government if this occurred

response_modes.reason: The relationship between Federation, the Constitution and the system of government is a complex layered concept — use a diagram or flowchart to make visible how the constitutional text produces the governmental structure.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two key features of Australia's system of government established at Federation.
Students explain how each feature is related to the Constitution.

nodes.label: Integrating the Federation story
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation and constitutional democratic system, identifying connections between the historical circumstances, the influential ideas and the resulting constitutional design.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how at least one key individual, one key event and one key idea each contributed to Federation and the Constitution.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the connections between the key individuals, events and ideas that led to Federation; describe how historical circumstances in the colonies created the conditions for Federation; explain how international ideas shaped the Constitution's design; and describe the democratic system of government that resulted.
wider: Evaluate which factor — individuals, events or ideas — was most significant in bringing about Federation, and justify the claim with reference to evidence
Assess how the founding principles and constitutional design of Australia have shaped its democratic system today — examining what has changed and what has remained constant

response_modes.reason: The integration task requires students to connect the narrative (who did what, when) to the analytical (why it happened and what it produced). Use a structured essay plan or annotated timeline to support this synthesis.

success_criteria: Students explain contributions of at least one individual, one event and one idea to Federation.
Students describe the democratic system of government that resulted from Federation.
Students use relevant historical and civics terms accurately (e.g. 'Federation', 'Constitution', 'constitutional monarchy', 'separation of powers').
